amendments.rule: A supplied English relative clause does not realize the article that governs it. Where the ASV renders an attributive participle as a finite clause — `τὴν δύναμιν τὴν ἐνεργουμένην` → *the power that worketh*, `τὸν καλούμενον` → *which is called* — the relativizer and any copula are helpers on the participle under rules 7 and 9, and the second attributive article stays its own `unrepresented` unit under rule 23. The test against rule 32 is whether the article governs an expressed head noun. `τῷ θεῷ τῷ κτίσαντι` → *God who created* has one, so the second article realizes nothing and *who* is the participle's helper; a bare `Τῷ δυναμένῳ` → *unto him that is able* has none, so the article is substantival and takes the pronoun itself. That test decides only the cases where a participle follows, because the participle is what carries the relativizer. It decides the **relativizer** alone and never the determiner, the two being separate questions: an article that **precedes** an expressed head noun of its own is that noun's determiner however the modifier standing between them is rendered, so where a participle intervenes the article takes the English *the* with any case preposition riding along under rule 21, and the participle still keeps the relativizer, any supplied copula and its own verb. `τοῖς κατοικοῦσιν ἐν τῇ Ἰουδαίᾳ ἀδελφοῖς` → *unto the brethren that dwelt in Judaea* gives *unto the* to the article, *that dwelt* to the participle and a bare *brethren* to the noun, exactly as rule 22's `τὴν ἀποκεκρυμμένην` → *even the wisdom that hath been hidden* divides a supplied nominal from the participle's own clause. The `unrepresented` article of this branch is the **second** attributive article, whose noun has already taken the determiner standing in front of it; an article with an English determiner of its own to carry is emptied neither by rule 23 nor by this rule. Where the article's modifier carries **no verb of its own** — a **prepositional phrase**, a bare **adverb**, or a **predicate adjective** — there is nothing there to carry the relativizer, so the article keeps the supplied relativizer whether or not it governs an expressed head noun, and the copula goes with the preposition, with the adverb or with the adjective: `τὰ στρατεύματα τὰ ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ` → *the armies which are in heaven* gives *which* to the second article and *are in* to `ἐν`, as `τὰ ἄνω` → *the things that are above* gives *the things that* to the article and *are above* to `ἄνω`. An adverb is no different from a prepositional phrase here, rule 53 already giving an adverbial predicate the supplied copula; and a **predicate adjective** is no different either, rule 53 naming an adjectival predicate beside those two, so a substantival article whose complement is an adjective keeps the antecedent pronoun and the relativizer together and the adjective keeps only the supplied copula and its own word: `Ὁ πιστὸς ἐν ἐλαχίστῳ` → *He that is faithful in a very little* gives *He that* to the article and *is faithful* to the adjective, exactly as `τῷ ἀλλοτρίῳ` → *that which is another's* and `τὸ ἐν ἀνθρώποις ὑψηλόν` → *that which is exalted among men* give *that which* to the article and the copula to the adjective. Rule 32's split, and rule 90's *He* / *that would*, are scoped in terms to a **participle**, which has a verb of its own to carry the relativizer, and are not a licence to strip the relativizer from an article whose complement is an adjective; where some other source token has already written the antecedent, rule 32's apposition clause empties the article and the relativizer falls to the adjective along with the copula, as `αὐτοῖς δὲ τοῖς κλητοῖς` → *unto them that are called* does. Where the article is substantival it takes the supplied nominal along with the relativizer under rule 22, headed on the nominal word and never on the determiner or on the relativizer. Which side takes the English *the* is decided by where the article stands, not by the relative clause. An article that **follows** its noun leaves the determiner on the noun, supplying one there when the noun is anarthrous: `καρπὸν δικαιοσύνης τὸν διὰ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ` → *the fruits of righteousness which are through Jesus Christ* gives *the fruits* to `καρπόν` and only *which* to `τόν`, as `κατὰ δικαιοσύνην τὴν ἐν νόμῳ` → *as touching the righteousness which is in the law* gives *the righteousness* to `δικαιοσύνην`. An article that **precedes** the noun it governs is that noun's own determiner and takes *the* along with the relativizer, headed on *the*, leaving the noun bare: `τὴν ἐκ θεοῦ δικαιοσύνην` → *the righteousness which is from God* gives the discontinuous *the … which* to `τήν` and *righteousness* to `δικαιοσύνην`, as `τὴν καθ' ὑμᾶς πίστιν` → *the faith … which is among you* does. That is rule 22's determiner clause holding where a head noun is expressed: the article carries the English determiner unless its own noun has already stood in front of it. An article left `unrepresented` in front of such a verbless modifier is right only where the ASV supplies no relative clause at all.
amendments.why: Rule 31's verbless-modifier carve-out enumerated only a prepositional phrase and a bare adverb, and a reader could take that list as closed. A substantival article whose complement is a predicate adjective is the same case by this rule's own stated reason — the modifier has no verb to carry the relativizer — and rule 53 already names an adjectival predicate beside the prepositional and the adverbial one. LUK.16 met the case three times and analysed it two ways because no rule named it: 16:12 and 16:15 followed rule 22's own example (τῷ → 'that which' whole on the article) while 16:10 followed rule 32's participial split. The amendment adds the adjective to the list with the two constructions from that chapter, states in terms that rules 32 and 90 are scoped to a participle, and preserves rule 32's apposition case, where an article emptied by another token leaves the relativizer to the adjective (τοῖς κλητοῖς → 'that are called'). Nothing in the precedent supplied contradicts it: the corpus carries 44 units of an article taking 'he that' headed on 'he' and 43 of 'that which' headed on 'that', and rule 77 records the substantival article as unanimous in taking 'that which' whole across all nine of its units.

amendments.rule: A substantival article before a participle splits; it does not absorb the clause. `οἱ κατοικοῦντες` → *they that dwell* is `οἱ` → *they* and `κατοικοῦντες` → *that dwell* headed on *dwell*, never one unit taking *they that*. The article supplies the pronoun and nothing else, because the participle is what the relative clause is predicated of. Where **another source token has already written that pronoun** — an expressed pronoun or noun standing in apposition to the article's phrase — nothing is left for the article to supply and it is its own `unrepresented` unit, the participle keeping the supplied relativizer along with any copula and its own verb: `τοῖς δὲ σῳζομένοις ἡμῖν` → *unto us who are saved* gives *unto us* to `ἡμῖν` under rule 21, nothing to the article, and *who are saved* to the participle headed on *saved*. That is rule 20's stated contrast holding where a participle rather than a noun follows the article, `Ὑμῖν … τοῖς ἔθνεσιν` → *to you that are Gentiles* leaving it empty because `ὑμῖν` has written the *you*, and it is the same reading an articular **adjective** in that apposition takes under rules 20 and 92, `αὐτοῖς δὲ τοῖς κλητοῖς` → *unto them that are called* giving *unto them* to `αὐτοῖς` and *that are called* to `κλητοῖς`. Rule 76's availability test does not reach this: an antecedent is the very word the relative clause is predicated of rather than an English word of some other role, so a pronoun that has written it is spent for this purpose and not available to the article. Rule 90 is the near contrast and is untouched: where the ASV writes only one English word for the pair that word is the article's, being pronoun and relativizer at once, and this clause reaches only a phrase for which the ASV writes more. Rule 22 is the contrast wherever no participle follows, and this rule's split is scoped in terms to a participle: what carries a supplied relativizer is a modifier with a verb of its own, so where the article's complement instead carries none — a **prepositional phrase**, a bare **adverb**, or a **predicate adjective** — the article carries *of him who* or *that which* whole and the modifier keeps only the supplied copula and its own word, as rule 31 has it. `οἱ μετ' αὐτοῦ` → *they … that are with him* keeps the discontinuous *they … that* on the article, since a prepositional phrase has no verb to carry a relativizer, and the copula goes with `μετά`; `Ὁ πιστός` → *He that is faithful* keeps *He that* on the article and gives *is faithful* to the adjective, and `τῷ ἀλλοτρίῳ` → *that which is another's* does the same. Where such an article is emptied by the apposition clause above, the relativizer falls to the adjective with the copula exactly as it falls to a participle. A reference comparison will report such an `unrepresented` article as a disagreement, and that report is not a correction.
amendments.why: This rule closed with 'That is the only configuration in which an article carries *of him who* or *that which* whole', naming the prepositional phrase alone. That sentence is false once rule 31's verbless-modifier branch is read as the class it argues for — rule 31 already added the bare adverb, and this amendment's companion adds the predicate adjective — and it is what licensed LUK.16.10's reading against the same chapter's 16:12 and 16:15. Leaving it standing while widening rule 31 would put the two rules in direct contradiction for whoever reads this one first. The replacement states the governing test (a modifier with a verb of its own carries the relativizer), names the three verbless modifiers, keeps the participial scope of the split, and preserves in full the apposition clause, rule 76's exclusion, rule 90's near contrast and the closing note on reference comparisons.

conventions: Substantival article whose complement is a predicate adjective: the article takes the English antecedent pronoun and the relativizer together, and the adjective takes the supplied copula and its own word. Ὁ πιστός -> 'He that' + 'is faithful' and ὁ ... ἄδικος -> 'he that' + 'is unrighteous' at 16:10, τῷ ἀλλοτρίῳ -> 'that which' + 'is another's' at 16:12, and τὸ ἐν ἀνθρώποις ὑψηλόν -> 'that which' + 'is exalted' at 16:15 are one analysis. An adjective has no verb of its own to carry the relativizer, so rule 32's pronoun-only split, which is scoped to a participle, does not reach it; rule 31's verbless-modifier branch and rule 22's τῷ -> 'that which' do. Every participial article in the chapter still splits under rule 32.

At 16:16 the ASV's 'the gospel of the kingdom of God is preached' renders εὐαγγελίζεται with a supplied nominal. The whole discontinuous frame 'the gospel of ... is preached' is folded onto the verb under rule 103's licensing test — no source token has spent that English, and the ASV's own margin 'Or, good tidings' shows it renders the εὐαγγελ- element — headed on the verbal core under rule 66. The 'of' inside that frame is licensed by the supplied 'gospel' and stays in the verb's unit under rule 21's frame clause; it is not a case preposition for ἡ βασιλεία, which is nominative and has no case for it to realize, so the article keeps a bare 'the' and βασιλεία a bare 'kingdom'.

report: One genuine cross-verse split, found and fixed: a substantival article whose complement is a predicate adjective, expanded into an English free relative, was analysed two ways. LUK.16.12 (τῷ ἀλλοτρίῳ -> 'that which is another's') and LUK.16.15 (τὸ ... ὑψηλόν -> 'that which is exalted') give the antecedent and the relativizer together to the article and only the copula to the adjective; LUK.16.10 gave the article a bare 'He'/'he' and put the relativizer on the adjective ('that is faithful', 'that is unrighteous'). The source shape is identical in all three and only the ASV's choice of free-relative idiom differs, which is rule 24's case. LUK.16.10 is patched to match, in both halves.

Direction of the fix taken from the contract rather than from a head-count: rule 22 lists τῷ -> 'that which' on the article as canonical, which is literally 16.12's construction, and rule 32 scopes the pronoun-only split to a participle on the stated ground that the participle is what carries the relativizer. An adjective has no verb of its own, so it falls with rule 31's prepositional phrase and bare adverb, and rule 53 already names an adjectival predicate beside those two.

Checked and found consistent, not split: every participle case takes rule 32's pronoun-only split (16.15 οἱ/δικαιοῦντες, 16.18 ὁ/ἀπολύων and ὁ/γαμῶν, 16.26 οἱ/θέλοντες), with 16.14 and 16.21 on rule 31's expressed-head-noun branch; both ἐνώπιον frames at 16.15 headed alike on 'sight' keeping the trailing 'of' (rules 71, 101); all article-plus-substantival-adjective units with a supplied nominal handled alike under rule 102 (16.11 'the ... riches', 16.21 'the ... man's', 16.22 'the ... man', 16.25 'things' twice); the existential rides with the verb at 16.1, 16.19 and 16.26 alike; every preverb particle rides inside its verb except where an expressed preposition's own gloss carries it (16.4 ἐκ -> 'out of', rule 106); the τις 'a certain X' frame is identical at 16.1, 16.19 and 16.20.

The table is blind to added units, so the chapter's one added unit was checked against every folded clause-introducer in it. 16.2 'that' stands over a finite indicative (ἀκούω) with no conjunction or participle to license it, so rule 86 makes it added; every folded introducer has a licensing token — 16.22's two 'that' on infinitives (rule 85), 16.26's repeated 'that' on μηδέ as the coordinated repetition of ὅπως (rules 86, 103), 16.17's repeated 'for' on the accusative subjects (rule 103). No hidden split there.

BSB disagreements: none is a genuine error. Five are articles emptied by a displacing possessive under rule 20 (16.2 τῆς 'thy stewardship', 16.5 τῷ 'my lord', 16.21 τῆς 'the rich man's table', 16.23 τοὺς 'his eyes', 16.24 τοῦ 'his finger'); 16.21 τῶν is a second attributive article whose relativizer is the participle's helper under rule 31; 16.23 ἀπὸ is pleonastic in ἀπὸ μακρόθεν -> 'afar off' under rule 34. All seven are the documented convention difference and none was touched.

Two conventions recorded — the article-plus-adjective division just settled, and 16.16's 'the gospel of ... is preached' frame, where the supplied nominal is folded onto εὐαγγελίζεται and the nominative ἡ keeps a bare 'the'. The 14 other repeated notes flagged by the validator all restate rules 20, 21, 22, 32, 51, 58, 72 or 88 verbatim and were left unlogged.

Two amendments returned rather than a new rule: rule 31's verbless-modifier carve-out names only a prepositional phrase and a bare adverb, and rule 32 then calls the prepositional phrase 'the only configuration' in which an article carries 'that which' whole. That sentence is what licensed 16.10's reading, so widening the list without correcting it would leave the misleading text in place for the next reader.
